messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 76
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: Widowed
- Occupation: Cashier
- Trauma Type: Civilian in war zone
- Pcl5: 67

# The Weight of What He Saw

Henryk is a 76-year-old Polish man who works part-time as a cashier at a small grocery store in the neighbourhood where he has lived for the past four decades. He is a slight man with careful eyes and deliberate hands, the kind of person who counts change twice and always says thank you. To the regular customers who pass through his checkout lane, he is simply a quiet, polite older gentleman. They do not know that when the automatic doors slide open and let in a gust of cold air, something in him still flinches.

Henryk was twelve years old when Soviet forces moved through his village in eastern Poland. He does not speak of it easily, and when he does, he speaks in fragments — as though the full story, assembled in one place, might be more than either of them could hold. What he describes is this: three days during which the world as he understood it ceased to exist. He watched soldiers drag his neighbour from his home. He heard sounds he could not then name and can now name too precisely. He hid beneath the floorboards of his family's barn with his younger sister pressed against him, her face buried in his chest so she would not make noise. He remembers the smell of the earth and the weight of the boards above him and how he did not cry, because crying felt like dying.

His family survived. They eventually emigrated. He married, raised children, built a life that looked, from the outside, entirely ordinary. His wife, Marta, died six years ago, and it was after her death that the past began moving toward him again — steadily, the way water rises.

He sleeps poorly now. He wakes most nights between two and four in the morning with his heart hammering and the absolute certainty that something terrible is happening just outside his awareness. The dreams are not always literal — sometimes it is just darkness and pressure and a sound he cannot locate — but they leave him sitting on the edge of his bed for an hour, unwilling to lie back down. He is exhausted most days, though he tells his children he sleeps fine.

At the store, he manages. The routine helps him — the scanner, the belt, the familiar faces. But there are moments that reach through the ordinary surface of things. A car backfiring in the parking lot sent him behind the counter last autumn, crouched and shaking, before he understood what had happened. A customer raised his voice at another register, and Henryk felt his body go somewhere far away, his hands moving through the motions of his work while his mind was underneath the floorboards, sixty-four years ago, holding his sister still. Afterwards he sat in the break room for twenty minutes and could not account for the time.

He avoids the news. He cannot watch anything involving soldiers or uniforms or crowds fleeing. When the war in Ukraine began, he stopped turning on the television entirely. He tells himself this is a reasonable choice, not a symptom. He is not sure he believes that.

What troubles him most, he says, is the guilt — not survivor's guilt exactly, but something adjacent to it. He wonders why he is still carrying this when so many others carried so much more. He thinks of his sister, who died young and never spoke of those days. He thinks of Marta, who knew enough not to ask certain questions. Without her, there is no one left who understood the particular shape of what he survived, and that aloneness has given the past more room to move.

He came to therapy, he says, because his daughter asked him to. He is not sure he deserves the attention. He is still not sure he deserves to have been the one who stayed quiet enough to survive.
